script.title: Demo 7 · Fine-tuning: a guest who isn't on the class list
script.case: A visitor speaks and is not enrolled: their lines must stay unknown and never be scored or credited to a student. Includes a claim the course slides don't cover.

lines.speaker: Prof Wynter
lines.text: Today we have a visitor from industry sitting in. We're discussing parameter efficient fine tuning. Instead of updating all the weights, what does LoRA do?

lines.speaker: Guest
lines.text: Hi everyone. In my team we use LoRA all the time. You freeze the base model and train two small low rank matrices that are added to the weight updates, so you only train a tiny fraction of the parameters.

lines.speaker: Prof Wynter
lines.text: Thank you. Students, why is that useful in practice?

lines.speaker: Tasmin
lines.text: It needs much less memory, and you can store one small adapter per task instead of a full copy of the model.

lines.speaker: Prof Wynter
lines.text: Good. What's the rank in LoRA, intuitively?

lines.speaker: Koh Qing Jia
lines.text: It's how many directions the update is allowed to change. A small rank like eight is often enough, and a larger rank gives more capacity but more parameters.

lines.speaker: Guest
lines.text: And quantising the base model to four bits on top of that is what QLoRA does.

lines.speaker: Tina
lines.text: I read that fine tuning with LoRA always beats retrieval augmented generation for factual questions.

lines.speaker: Prof Wynter
lines.text: I don't think the evidence supports always. For facts that change, retrieval is usually the better tool. Let's stop there.
